summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy was criminalised in Mongolia in 1961 and decriminalised in 1993, when all references were removed from the Criminal Code. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited across several separate instruments rather than a single equality statute. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in effect since 1 July 2017, bans discrimination on both grounds. Article 1.3.2 of the revised Criminal Law adopted on 3 December 2015 bars discrimination in criminalisation and sentencing on grounds including sexual and gender orientation. Article 6 of the Labour Code, since 2022, bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Protections remain fragmented and no comprehensive equality law is in place.

Hate-crime and hate-speech provisions expressly cover gender identity. The Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 included gender identity as a protected ground for hate crimes; the code was scheduled to take effect on 1 September 2016 and was postponed to 1 July 2017. Section 10(1)(2)(14) of the Penal Code aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is outlawed.

A June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law allows transgender people to change their legal gender on birth certificates or citizen identification cards following sex reassignment surgery.

Marriage is defined in Article 16(11) of the Constitution as based on the equality and mutual consent of a man and a woman who have reached the age determined by law, with State protection for family, motherhood and child. Same-sex relationships are not recognised and same-sex couple households are ineligible for the same protections as opposite-sex couples; no union recognition of any kind is available. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore has no legal standing for that partnership.

A residual offence addressing 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' remains on the statute book despite the absence of laws specifically criminalising homosexuality.

Enforcement of hate-crime provisions remains weak in practice. As of August 2018 the LGBT Centre was training more than 300 police officers, prosecutors and judges on hate-crime handling, and after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman in 2019 the Centre trained 500 or more police officers, prosecutors and judges on the 2017 criminal code's hate-crime provisions. The force adopted guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identity documents. Despite this training, local reports and activists say police continue to disregard or not take seriously complaints of hate crimes against LGBTQ people, and attacks often result in no punishment.

Documented violence against transgender people includes a September 2009 incident in which three transgender women were kidnapped in broad daylight at a promenade in Ulaanbaatar by a hyper-nationalist group, driven to a cemetery on the city outskirts, beaten, sexually assaulted and forced to perform sexual acts on the perpetrators as a warning. The attack was not reported to police for fear of victimisation and reprisal. In February 2014 a gay man was sexually assaulted by a neo-Nazi group, and in 2001 a lesbian woman was raped, abducted and stabbed by two men; such violence is often not reported to police.

Violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people are fairly common and often unreported. Mongolian culture is and has remained strongly heteronormative, and despite the 2017 protections, ostracism, harassment and violence persist both socially and systemically. A 2019 report found that 79% of LGBTQ-identified young people experienced bullying, discrimination or ostracism, with several LGBTQ students reporting discrimination and bullying at schools.

Community visibility is limited. The scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism; a 2008 account describes two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees fear being outed. LGBT groups can register as organisations. The LGBT Centre in Ulaanbaatar has advocated publicly and organised a Pride event in 2018, and trans man Anaraa Nyamdorj, who came out in 2004 and began transition in 2011, co-founded and advises the Centre.
tangentialFactors:
Public attitudes show a documented split along lines of gender presentation. A December 2018 social experiment in Ulaanbaatar placed three LGBTQ people, a gay man, a lesbian and a transgender man, roadside to observe reactions; online responses ranged from death threats to negative comments to positive ones, and the exercise showed that the public were more welcoming of the lesbian and the trans man than of the gay man.

The sex education curriculum introduced in 1998 includes discussion of LGBTQ and sexual health issues, though teachers may choose whether to cover these topics.

A 2013 report found that over 73% of LGBTQ Mongolians had considered suicide due to social nonacceptance and intolerance. A 2012 National Human Rights Commission survey of LGBT people, an LGBT-wide population rather than a trans-specific one, found almost 80% had experienced broadly categorised 'human-rights abuse' in the preceding three years, with almost three-quarters having considered suicide; both figures are historical and do not measure current trans prevalence.

May 2014: the Government announced it would consider anti-discrimination legislation following public outcry. No comprehensive equality law has since been enacted.
localsOnly:
Trans Mongolian residents may change their legal gender on birth certificates or citizen identification cards under the June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law, conditional on having undergone sex reassignment surgery.

Article 6 of the Labour Code, in force since 2022, gives residents a discrimination claim in employment on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in force since 1 July 2017, provides a parallel prohibition, and Section 10(1)(2)(14) aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation.

Police guidelines require officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of the gender marker on identity documents, following training delivered by the LGBT Centre after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman.

Same-sex couples cannot marry and are ineligible for the family, motherhood and child protections the Constitution extends to opposite-sex couples; no alternative union recognition exists.
outOfScopeNotes:
The ADB's legal-status survey for Asia and the Pacific carries no finding on record for Mongolia, so no comparative legal assessment from that source is available.

Whether the residual 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' offence has been applied against consensual adult conduct since decriminalisation in 1993 is not sourced here.

Whether the training of police, prosecutors and judges on hate-crime handling has produced measurable changes in charging or conviction rates is unresolved in the available material; the sources document the training and continued reports of complaints being disregarded, but no outcome data.

Current registration status and activity level of LGBT organisations beyond the LGBT Centre's documented work are not sourced.
